articles.title: Critics celebrate Céline Dion's 'risky' comeback show in Paris
articles.summary: The iconic Canadian singer kicked off her long-awaited comeback show in Paris on Saturday, after a six-year hiatus due to health issues.
articles.body:
Iconic Canadian pop singer Céline Dion has kicked off her long-awaited comeback show in Paris on Saturday, after a six-year hiatus due to health issues.

The 58-year-old superstar was diagnosed with a rare neurological disorder called stiff person syndrome in 2022, which forced her to pull back from touring.

Dion, one of the best-selling musical artists of all time, has not performed a full show since a 2020 concert in New Jersey - the last before the Covid pandemic cut her tour short. In 2024, she performed just one song at the Paris Olympics closing ceremony.

Saturday marked the first of Dion's 26-show residency at the Paris La Défense Arena, Europe's largest covered concert arena.

"I made a promise," she told the Paris audience of about 30,000 people in her emotional return.

"I made a promise to come back, to be back on stage. And here I am. Singing for you, and singing for me," she said.

"I am everything I am because you loved me," she told the crowd.

She also broke down in tears after finishing a song, telling the audience: "I had promised myself not to cry."

"But I'm so happy to see you all. I missed you."

They weren't the only tears of the night, as the star appeared to be overcome with emotion several times.

Dion will be performing in Paris throughout September and October and into the New Year.

The Mirror's Lucy Needham noted that the singer was 50 minutes late to start, and may have needed extra time to "compose herself" for the "emotionally charged return".

"Eyes-brimming, the veteran singer gave herself little nods of approval after every line, before finally breaking down at the end of the track, seemingly overwhelmed at having made it through."

After beginning her set in a black gown, she later changed into a trouser suit "to show off some of those signature kooky dance moves," says Needham, adding that she appeared "to be having the time of her life, gyrating and slapping her thighs with glee".

The night was a "a tense, tearful, joyous affair probably even more so for the singer than for her loyal audience," writes The Telegraph's Neil McCormick .

She started out slow, he says. "Her voice sounded fragile and exposed, but at least it was her distinctive voice, not some autotuned approximation."

"At first, she was clearly struggling to hold herself together," he continues. "Her vocals wobbled dangerously, as if about to crack or collapse. But she was gaining confidence with every moment back on stage."

She broke down in tears as the audience roared in approval after the first song, and addressed the crowd in both French and English during the set.

"This was a high-stakes, high-wire return, perhaps the riskiest comeback in the history of showbusiness," McCormick continues, referring to her health condition.

But he concludes: "I honestly think I prefer this less superhuman Céline. Her voice is still great, but a bit more raw and real, with a rougher tone, less smoothness in the runs and more edge to her whoops and shrieks."

Sarah Leavitt, reporting from Paris for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) , said the crowd "was left without words" by the stunning performance.

She noted that she didn't want to cry, but "of course she cried right away."

Dion also "endeared herself" to the crowd by saying during one song that she wanted to stop and start over.

Will Hodgkinson at the Times of London writes in his review, "miraculously, her art will go on," that the performance was "overwhelming".

She "looked suitably humbled and tearful" as she emerged, he said, going on to praise the stage direction.

"Truly, she was throwing the love at the crowd, who threw it right back at her. There was no holding back. It was quite overwhelming, actually," he writes.

The performance was "complete with both costume, key change and air of tragic, important romance".

"Céline Dion's strength lies in being a diva with the common touch while being as French as they get, even if she is Canadian. She fulfilled that role with all the verve you could hope for," writes Hodgkinson.

"The concert had a spiritual feel, with visual interludes steeped in biblical imagery alluding to a pilgrimage," Elsa Keslassy writes for Variety.

In video clips, Dion is seen wandering in a desert. "The set design was highly cinematic, with a monumental staircase sweeping up one side and a moon dominating the stage, while the backdrop appeared to have a stark, almost brutalist gray texture."

The star, known for power ballads like My Heart Will Go On and Because You Loved Me, has said she will not let her diagnosis control her life.

"The way I see it, I have two choices. Either I train like an athlete and work super hard, or I switch off and it's over," she told French Vogue magazine in 2024.

"I've chosen to work with all my body and soul, from head to toe, with a medical team."

When Dion announced the first leg of her Paris residency back in March, nine million fans signed up for early access tickets to the concerts, French outlet FRI reported.

The shows sold out so fast that her management company soon announced an additional 10 shows scheduled for May 2027, which have also since sold out.

Fans who were unable to snag tickets to one of the highly anticipated shows have not been left out entirely - events honouring Dion's comeback have dominated Paris in recent weeks.

Céline Dion tribute boat cruises on Seine - complete with costume contests, sing-alongs, DJ sets, are happening throughout September.

Ahead of Saturday's show, fans gathered outside Dion's Paris hotel, LeRoyal Monceau, as early as 06:00 local time to catch a glimpse of the star.

Paris City Hall organised a massive karaoke event on Friday night, attended by thousands, to celebrate Dion's return to the stage.

"I couldn't get tickets to the concert. I'm still keeping my fingers crossed and hoping, but I thought to myself: at least I can share a moment here with all the fans," Rania, a participant at the event, told Reuters.

Earlier this week, thousands of fans also gathered at a historic theatre in central Paris for two nights of karaoke and activities inspired by Dion's music.

And Paris venues and night clubs are hosting Dion-themed events around the city on Saturday night for fans who couldn't get tickets to the actual show.

articles.title: Why Spain’s new Sahrawi citizenship law matters to Morocco
articles.summary: The new citizenship bill for Sahrawis touches a sensitive fault line in Madrid’s ties with Rabat.
articles.body:
Spain’s Congress has approved a bill that would open a special route to Spanish citizenship for Sahrawis born in Western Sahara while the disputed territory was under Spanish occupation.

The bill passed by 168 votes to 31, with 145 abstentions. It must still go through the Senate before it can become law.

So what exactly would the measure do, and why is Morocco watching it closely?

The proposed law would allow people born in Western Sahara before September 29, 1977, to apply for Spanish nationality through a special procedure without having to meet the normal residency requirements. First-degree descendants would also be covered.

It would also shorten the duration of the residence requirement for eligible Sahrawis legally living in Spain. Instead of the usual 10 years, they would be able to apply after two years.

Supporters describe the measure as a way of addressing what they see as a historical injustice.

Spain was the colonial power in Western Sahara until it ended its administration of the territory in 1976. The territory has remained disputed ever since, with Morocco considering it part of its sovereignty, while the separatist Polisario Front seeks independence.

The law would not change the territorial status of Western Sahara. It would not recognise an independent Sahrawi state, nor would Spanish citizenship give its holders sovereignty over the territory.

The concern in Rabat is instead about the relationship the law could create between Spain and people with direct links to Western Sahara.

Reuters has reported that between 70,000 and 110,000 people could eventually qualify, although estimates vary. Anyone who obtains Spanish nationality would also become a European Union citizen and acquire the rights that come with that status.

Potential beneficiaries could include eligible Sahrawis living in Western Sahara as well as members of the Sahrawi refugee population around Tindouf in Algeria, where the Polisario Front is based.

For Morocco, that could mean a larger community of Spanish and EU citizens with personal or family ties to an issue at the centre of its relationship with Madrid.

The bill comes after a significant change in Spain’s policy towards Western Sahara.

In 2022, Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s government backed Morocco’s autonomy proposal for the territory, describing it as the most serious, realistic and credible basis for resolving the dispute.

That decision helped repair relations between Madrid and Rabat after a major diplomatic crisis. Since then, the two countries have strengthened cooperation on migration, security, trade and other areas.

The new citizenship measure does not formally change Spain’s support for the autonomy proposal. Madrid can argue that supporting autonomy as a political solution is one matter, while dealing with the consequences of its former colonial rule is another.

But the two issues are difficult to separate completely from Morocco’s perspective because both concern Western Sahara.

The bill has also divided Spain’s political parties.

The governing Socialist Party and its allies in Sumar supported it. The conservative People’s Party abstained, while Vox voted against it.

The disagreement has centred partly on how Spain should address the legacy of its former rule in Western Sahara and on the legal route proposed for granting nationality.

The debate is important to the Moroccan side because it shows that the measure is not simply a technical change to Spanish nationality law. It has also become part of a discussion inside Spain about its colonial past and its relationship with Western Sahara.

Moroccan and international media have also focused on the measure. While Moroccan media have highlighted its potential implications for Spain’s policy towards Western Sahara and its relations with Rabat, Reuters has reported that the move could further strain relations between Spain and Morocco.

No. The proposed nationality route does not recognise the Polisario Front or an independent Sahrawi state.

Nor does acquiring Spanish citizenship indicate support for the Polisario. Nationality is a legal status, and Sahrawis hold different political positions.

The connection to the Polisario is nevertheless relevant because many Sahrawi refugees live around Tindouf, where the Polisario has its headquarters and administers the refugee camps.

If eligible people from those communities acquire Spanish nationality, they would become Spanish and EU citizens while retaining their existing personal and political identities.

Why is Spain referring to its colonial past?

Spain was the colonial power in Western Sahara until it ended its administration of the territory in 1976.

Supporters of the bill argue that people born in the territory during Spanish rule were left in a difficult legal position after Spain withdrew. They therefore present the measure as a way of addressing what they consider a historical wrong.

Spain has used historical ties in nationality policy before.

In 2015, it introduced a procedure allowing Sephardic Jews who could establish their Sephardic origin and a special connection with Spain to apply for Spanish nationality. The measure was linked to the expulsion of Jews from Spain beginning in 1492.

That precedent is relevant to the Moroccan debate because Spain has previously used historical ties to establish a special route to nationality.

This is where the issue becomes particularly sensitive for Morocco.

Morocco considers Ceuta and Melilla an integral part of its territory and sovereignty. The two cities are located on Morocco’s northern coast in North Africa and are under Spanish administration.

Spain rejects Morocco’s claim and considers the cities Spanish territory. Successive Spanish governments have maintained that their sovereignty over Ceuta and Melilla is not negotiable.

The Moroccan argument here could be about how historical ties are treated.

If Spain can draw on its historical and colonial relationship with Western Sahara to create a special nationality route for Sahrawis, and has previously used historical ties with Sephardic Jews, whose connection to Spain dates back more than five centuries, Morocco could ask why its own historical and geographical relationship with Ceuta and Melilla should be considered irrelevant when it makes its claim to sovereignty over the two cities.

For eight centuries, Muslim dynasties, including the Almoravids and Almohads, ruled parts of the Iberian Peninsula.

Morocco’s potential argument is therefore narrower: if historical ties can help establish present-day legal rights, then history and geography can also form part of the case it makes about two cities located on the North African coast.

The citizenship measure would not change who controls Western Sahara, determine the territory’s final status or alter the United Nations-led political process. Nor does it, in itself, change Spain’s official position in support of Morocco’s autonomy proposal.

Its significance lies mainly in the relationship between Spain and Morocco. The measure brings Spain’s colonial history in Western Sahara into a broader domestic political debate, raising questions about how that history should be addressed and what its growing political significance could mean for the delicate relationship between Madrid and Rabat.

articles.title: Thaw in ties deserves to be cherished, says Xi; border peace is essential: PM Modi
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Chinese President Xi Jinping told PM Narendra Modi the current momentum in bilateral ties anchored in resumption of institutional exchanges.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Chinese President Xi Jinping told PM Narendra Modi the current momentum in bilateral ties anchored in resumption of institutional exchanges, expanding cooperation agenda and increasing trade is hard-won and deserves to be cherished, as both sides looked to reinforce the thaw in the relationship with another meeting between the leaders.While PM Modi joined Xi in welcoming the “steady progress” in bilateral relations, he underlined India’s position that peace and tranquility in border areas will act as an essential basis for continued development of the relationship.The leaders met on the margins of the BRICS summit for what was their third bilateral meeting in 2 years, starting with Kazan in 2024 and Tianjin last year. In their 40-minute meeting, the first on Indian soil in 7 years, PM Modi and Xi agreed that both countries should take a strategic and long-term perspective of their ties and differences should not cause disputes.Xi reiterated India and China are partners, not rivals, but the Indian readout on this occasion, unlike the Tianjin statement by India last year, skipped mention of that formulation.PM Modi also underlined the need for both sides to observe existing agreements and understandings on border-related issues. An Indian readout said they expressed commitment to a fair, reasonable, and mutually acceptable resolution of the boundary question proceeding from the political perspective of their overall bilateral relations and the long-term interests of the two peoples.The PM also raised the issue of India’s trade deficit with China and the need for supply chain predictability. According to the Indian side, they underlined the need to address each other’s concerns, including structural trade imbalance and supply chain issues, and facilitation of meaningful and predictable market access.Since their meeting in Kazan in 2024, which marked the end of the eastern Ladakh border standoff, three rounds of Special Representatives talks on the boundary question have taken place. In the last meeting, they agreed to advance negotiations for an early and substantial harvest of boundary delimitation and border management.PM Modi and Xi noted the progress in people-to-people ties and underscored the need to further promote cultural exchanges, business linkages and greater mobility between the two countries, said the Indian side. “Prime Minister highlighted that both sides must be guided by three mutuals- mutual respect, mutual sensitivity and mutual interest,” said the readout, adding that they agreed to expand common ground on regional and global issues, and in addressing challenges.In his remarks, Xi proposed more rational strategic assessment of the relationship looking forward, win-win cooperation, mutual respect and understanding and inclusive multilateral cooperation.A Chinese readout of the meeting quoted PM Modi as saying that India follows an independent foreign policy and its ties with Beijing are not influenced by any third country. It also said that Modi told Xi India’s position on Taiwan and Tibet-related issues have not changed and it will not allow anyone to carry out anti-China activities.The Chinese foreign ministry had attributed the same remark to external affairs minister S Jaishankar after his meeting with counterpart Wang Yi in July this year. articles.title: Iraq seizes drone-launching platform used for targeting Saudi oil pipeline
articles.summary: Saudi authorities trace the launch site to Maysan province in southeastern Iraq, near the Iranian border.
articles.body:
Iraqi authorities have said their security forces have located and seized a drone-launching platform allegedly used in an attack that struck Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline.

In a statement published by the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA) on Saturday, Lieutenant General Saad Maan, head of Iraq’s Security Media Cell, said that an intelligence and security task force had tracked down and seized the launch equipment.

He also said that forensic and technical experts were continuing work to identify those behind the attack and that Iraq’s commander-in-chief had approved an Iranian request to join the investigation and review its findings.

Baghdad is maintaining direct communication with Saudi authorities to share intelligence, Maan said.

“Iraq adopts the principle of ‘preventive sovereignty’, which means not only preventing attacks on our territory, but also not allowing our land to be a launching pad against any other country, or for Iraq to be part of a proxy war,” he said, as quoted by INA.

Several people were injured after several drones launched from Iraq struck the East-West pipeline in the Riyadh and Medina regions on Thursday, Saudi authorities said. The pipeline, which carries about 4 to 5 percent of the global oil supply and allows Saudi Arabia to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, was shut down as a precaution.

The kingdom also said it had decided against retaliating for now, following a request from Baghdad.

Saudi authorities traced the launch site to Maysan province in southeastern Iraq , a region near the Iranian border where Iran-aligned militias have long maintained a presence.

Al Jazeera’s Mohammed Rammal reported that the Iraqi authorities had pointed to the al-Tayeb border district in northeastern Maysan province near the Sheeb crossing, east of Amara, and encompassing both the Duwayrij River and Tayeb Island as the likely launch site.

Rammal said that with the targeted areas covering roughly 1,100 kilometres (684 miles) from Medina and 800km (497 miles) from Riyadh, the attack likely involved “not tactical drones, but long-range, advanced ones”.

Iraqi army spokesman Sabah al-Numan said earlier on Saturday that security and intelligence agencies were pursuing operations to arrest all those involved.

Following the strike, Iraqi authorities temporarily closed several border crossings with Iran, including Shalamcheh, Chazabeh and Mandali, for security inspections before partially reopening them for humanitarian traffic.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi reshuffled military commanders in border regions, including Maysan province, in the wake of the attack.

Al Jazeera correspondent Samer al-Kubaisi named the Maysan operations commander and the provincial police chief as among those dismissed, with a group of security commanders in the province now under investigation over the attacks.

Political analyst Salim Zakhour told Al Jazeera that Saudi Arabia “did not go toward direct escalation on the ground”, but instead sought “political containment through the Iraqi government”.

He said the developments of the past few days are “extremely complex for Saudi Arabia”, pointing to the Houthis’ advance towards Bab al-Mandeb alongside the East-West oil pipeline strike.

This leaves Riyadh in a major defensive position, requiring “real, practical steps to deter these attempts,” Zakhour added.

articles.title: One dead, more than 30 missing after Vanuatu ferry sinks, PM’s office says
articles.summary: Rescuers continue searching for survivors as the government scales back operations in open waters.
articles.body:
At least one person has died and more than 30 remain missing after a ferry sank off the coast of Vanuatu, Prime Minister Jotham Napat’s office has said in a statement.

The MV Matui, an inter-island ferry, sank in bad weather on Friday while sailing between the islands of Ambae and Santo, in Vanuatu’s north, according to New Zealand’s public broadcaster RNZ.

Of the dozens of crew members and passengers on board, 15 have been accounted for alive, Napat’s office said in a statement posted on Facebook, with search and rescue operations continuing.

The Pacific nation’s government said search efforts “in open waters” were being scaled back “whilst efforts move toward a search along the south-east coast, where currents may have carried survivors”.

It said the sinking “appears to be the result of strong winds and marine warnings not being heeded, and possibly of negligence including overloading of the vessel”, adding that a full investigation would follow to establish the facts and prevent a repeat.

Vanuatu police, the country’s Maritime Safety Authority and the ferry’s operator, Tui Shipping Agency, did not immediately respond to requests for comment, the Reuters news agency reported.

articles.title: Starting September, Google is moving 'AI responsibility' team out of Google DeepMind; here's what VP Helen King told employees in an email
articles.summary: Tech News News: Google is moving its roughly 90-person AI responsibility team out of Google DeepMind as part of a wider reorganisation at the company, according to an.
articles.body: Google is moving its roughly 90-person AI responsibility team out of Google DeepMind as part of a wider reorganisation at the company, according to an internal email viewed by The Wall Street Journal. Reportedly starting in September, the team will move to Google’s global affairs organisation, which handles lobbying and public policy. The change comes as Google is bringing DeepMind more closely into the wider company structure. The move has raised concerns among some employees about whether the team will continue to have enough access to DeepMind’s AI research.Google DeepMind AI responsibility team to move in SeptemberThe AI responsibility unit, which has about 90 employees, is expected to join Google’s global affairs organisation at the beginning of September. The team is led by Helen King, a vice president at Google DeepMind. In an email to employees, King described the change as part of a broader shift in how DeepMind is organised.“GDM is moving into a more typical PA setup with central teams in central Google,” King wrote. PA refers to “product area”, a term Google uses for major divisions of the company.Other teams, including HR and policy groups, are also being moved out of DeepMind and into central Google.Employees raise concerns over AI safety researchThe restructuring has raised concerns among some members of the AI responsibility team, according to two current DeepMind employees cited by the Journal. Employees have questioned whether moving the team away from DeepMind could affect its ability to carry out independent research. They have also raised concerns about losing access to information about the work being done by teams developing Google’s Gemini AI models.The concerns come as governments, researchers and the public continue to examine the risks and wider effects of increasingly capable AI systems.The team works on several areas linked to AI safety and responsible AI. According to the people cited by the Journal, some teams test Google’s AI models for chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear risks. Other researchers study how people interact with AI systems and examine the psychological effects of chatbots.Employees are concerned that reduced access to DeepMind researchers could make it harder to identify safety questions linked to new AI models.Helen King reassures Google employeesKing told employees that the restructuring would not change the team's day-to-day work or its main mission. She said the team would continue to focus on emerging and frontier issues in responsible AI. Publishing research and taking part in external events would also remain supported.King also said the team would retain access to DeepMind, along with its computing resources and head count.“Demis still cares a lot about Responsible AI and is still planning to be involved,” King wrote.Google said the move is intended to bring its AI safety and responsibility work closer together across the company. “Many teams across Google work on AI safety and responsibility, and by bringing our AI responsibility teams closer together we’re strengthening their ability to inform safety for our models and products,” a Google spokesperson said.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: Essay: ‘I stood and watched a place I loved vanish’
articles.summary: For 11 years I stayed in the same hotel during my visits to Syabru Besi, a small Nepali town that sat high on a ridge where the trail to the Langtang Valley begins.
articles.body: For 11 years I stayed in the same hotel during my visits to Syabru Besi, a small Nepali town that sat high on a ridge where the trail to the Langtang Valley begins. Langtang is one of Nepal’s most beautiful trekking routes, a path that climbs until the valley opens up and the mountains fill every direction, close enough to feel like you could reach out and touch them. In all that time, the hotel room never changed, and neither did the sound. At night I could hear the Trishuli River, but I could never see it. It ran down the gorge, far below the village. Just to catch a glimpse of that thin silver line of water, you had to walk out to the edge of the village, lean over the ridge, and search for it. Syabru Besi held onto itself in a way almost nowhere in Nepal manages now. Same shopfronts. Same faces. There had been no coffee in the town at all on my first visit in 2014. By 2025 the hotel owner was telling me, a little proud, “Syabru has changed now, there’s a café up the road. Better coffee than anything you’ll get in the trendiest corner of Kathmandu.” There was a famous momo place, too, selling steaming hot dumplings that dripped with local flavor. On my last visit it was packed, every table taken. Syabru Besi had stopped being just a stop on the road to the mountains. It had become a small town climbing, slowly, toward something better. Then on August 31, 2026, I walked into that market and found no one. I had come this time not as a trekker but as part of a CNN team covering the disaster in Nepal. I had watched the footage. It did not prepare me. The momo restaurant still stood, the building anyway, and it was empty. The café was gone. And the hotel I had slept in for 11 years, the one where I could hear the Trishuli without ever seeing it, was not there at all. The river had taken it. The Trishuli was closer than I had seen it in all those years, having risen what looked to me like 260 feet (80 meters) or more. Never did I imagine standing in Syabru Besi with the Trishuli lapping that close to my feet. It had climbed all the way up to meet me. A 45-mile wound Syabru Besi was only where the grief started. I traveled the corridor up from Galchi toward Rasuwagadhi, past Betrawati, Mailung, Shantibazar, Timure, Trishuli Bazaar – towns with names, with shopkeepers, with morning routines. At every turn of the river the same thing had happened: both banks stripped to bare rock and gray water. Not damaged. Erased. Where houses and tea shops and bus parks had stood, there was now a riverbed giving off a bad smell, and you could hardly believe this rubble had been a living market a week before. The flood came off the China-Nepal border on the morning of 26 August. Weather stations near the border had logged little or no rain. Nepal’s Department of Hydrology and Meteorology believes a glacier snapped, triggering a landslide that formed a lake which burst its banks, throwing a wall of water and debris down the Bhotekoshi River. The glacier gave way at 8:37 that morning, according to the US Geological Survey, and within 13 minutes the flood had destroyed the river gauge at the Syabru Besi hydrological station. Not hours. Minutes. The toll is staggering and still rising. The disaster struck dozens of settlements along a 45-mile (72-kilometer) stretch of the Trishuli, killing at least 1,300 people. Some of the dead were carried 150 kilometers downstream, into India. Thousands remain missing. A government damage committee counted 7,570 buildings destroyed across five districts; the finance minister has since estimated the full reconstruction cost could reach $5 billion. Engineers, hydropower workers, customs staff and traders are among the missing, and so are people who were very close to me. I keep their faces out of this essay, because their families are still waiting, and hope is a fragile and private thing. A warning had come before. In July 2025 a flood off the Lhende River poured into this same Bhotekoshi River, killing at least nine people and tearing away the Miteri friendship bridge that ties Nepal to China. We rebuilt. A temporary Bailey bridge went up. Trade came limping back. Fourteen months later, the mountain sent something far bigger, and this time there was nothing left to rebuild. The corridor that carried the country To grasp what the Trishuli corridor was, you have to understand that, in Nepal, a road is never only a road. The Pasang Lhamu Highway, and the river running beside it, made these small towns. People came down out of the hills for the market, the connection, the opening the road gave them, and Betrawati and Trishuli Bazaar filled up with them. Opportunity built these places, and now both the opportunity and the places are gone. Downstream, the disaster sank a section of the Prithvi Highway at Krishnabhir, cutting the main artery between Kathmandu and the rest of the country, and left the whole Langtang Valley severed, some 450 people reachable only by helicopter or a two-day walk. The corridor carried the country’s northern trade as well. The Rasuwagadhi–Kerung crossing is Nepal’s largest China-facing customs point, handling roughly $563 million in imports last fiscal year: computers, machinery, electronics, garments, the goods that stock Kathmandu’s shelves before the festivals. About 19% of everything Nepal imports comes from China, and a large share of that overland flow moved through this valley. Even before August, none of Nepal’s three major China trade points were fully working. Landslides had shut Tatopani. Korala was clearing two or three trucks a day at 4,650 meters. Rasuwagadhi was still limping from the previous year’s flooding. Now the busiest of the three is a gash in the ground. Open up that one fact and the cost inside it is enormous, for traders, for prices, for a small economy that could not absorb such a loss even in a good year. We bet the country on these rivers Here is what keeps an economist like myself up at night. Nepal has wagered its future on the very water now ripping through its valleys. Hydropower, next to remittances, is one of the few genuine engines this economy has. Consider how total the wager is. Almost all of Nepal’s electricity comes from hydropower. Nepal’s installed capacity has climbed to somewhere between 3,400 and 3,900 MW, nearly all of it hydro, with more than 4,000 MW under construction and a pipeline the industry prices in the tens of billions of dollars. By 2029, installed capacity is expected to triple to almost 12,000 MW, and by 2035, the latest climate pledge could see that more than double again. Nearly every one of those megawatts sits in a river gorge like this one. And the rivers are turning on the very projects built to harness them. The flood disaster damaged or destroyed 13 hydropower projects along the Bhotekoshi and the Trishuli, knocking out 12% of the country’s total electricity capacity. Last week, as I stood beside the muddied remains of the Trishuli 3A hydropower station that had, days before, been lighting homes in Kathmandu, I thought about the rest of the projects upstream on the Bhotekoshi, the ones drawn up for basins we have not yet learned to be afraid of. If a glacial collapse can wipe out a 45-mile corridor in 13 minutes, then what are we building, and where? Civilization does not always return to the river I was raised on the idea that human civilization began on riverbanks, that water is where people gather and cities take hold. Standing in a bed of boulders where families used to sleep, I have come to believe the reverse now holds here. They are not going back. A life cannot be rebuilt on a floor of stone. For a country earning around $1,500 a head, putting Betrawati, Timure, Shantibazar and Mailung back where they physically stood is not merely hard. It cannot be done. The ground itself is gone, turned into channel. Nor does the harm stop at the flood line. The downstream markets, the ones the water only scared rather than destroyed, will carry the corridor’s death in lost trade and thinning footfall for years. So, the real question is not whether civilization comes back to the Trishuli corridor. It will not. The question is how we shield the civilizations along the other corridors, because there are so many of them. Nepal is a country of rivers, more than eight major basins, and along nearly every one of them sit towns exactly like Syabru Besi: ordinary, hopeful, set a little too near water that keeps rising. Far above them the glaciers are melting, and the lakes they feed are swelling and breaking loose. China itself warned on August 31 of a continuing risk from fresh glacier collapse along the same border, even as we were still counting our dead. What used to be a catastrophe that came once in a generation is turning into something we brace for every monsoon. Nepal’s own disaster report recorded more than 32,000 small- and large-scale disaster incidents between 2018 and 2024, roughly 5,400 a year, a curve bending the wrong way. The disaster that manufactures poverty Inside the loud catastrophe there is a quieter one, and as an economist it may be the one that frightens me most. Every disaster like this one manufactures poor Nepalis. A flood takes the house, the crop, the livestock, the shop, the savings. The family borrows to rebuild, then borrows again to eat, and by the time the next disaster lands they are weaker than they were. Nepal’s poverty rate fell from 41.8% in 1995 to about 20% by 2023, but that progress has stalled precisely as disasters have multiplied. In the late 1990s poverty was dropping by 1.36 percentage points a year. But those gains were built on remittances, not on resilient growth, and disasters are eating those gains one valley at a time. Across the last 12 years, the span that holds the 2015 earthquake and the Covid pandemic, it has crept down by just 0.41 points a year. The 2015 earthquake alone shoved as many as 982,000 people back below the poverty line. The Melamchi flood of 2021 set some in the worst-hit ward back even further, thrusting more into multidimensional poverty – poorer not just in income but in education, health and living standards. Our poverty gains were built on remittances, not on resilient growth, and disasters are eating those gains one valley at a time. The Rasuwa flood has not only ended lives. It has quietly begun turning middle-income families along the Trishuli into poor ones. And yet, what gives me hope is the resilience of ordinary Nepalis. We have come through the 2015 earthquake, the Covid years, the Gen-Z uprising, and after each blow this country has somehow risen back stronger, its people returning to their lives and their livelihoods faster than anyone had a right to expect. I stood in a riverbed that had been a town that I loved, and I still believe we will come back from this one too. But belief is not a plan, and resilience is no substitute for support. We will need it, for the families still combing the downstream banks, for the towns that must be relocated rather than rebuilt, and for a small mountain nation that did almost nothing to warm the planet now seeing its glaciers melt above its own people’s heads. Because that is the whole of it. A climate shifting faster than we are ready for. Glacial lakes filling quietly in the peaks above towns that are still asleep, towns that do not yet know their names are on a list. The dead we have already counted, and the far larger number still standing in the water’s path. Trade routes cut, an economy left exposed, an energy future we are gambling on with the risk folded quietly into the wager. I stood and watched a place I loved vanish. And I keep coming back to the one thing I cannot shake: this is a country that keeps returning to the water, for its towns, its trade, its power, its whole idea of the future, while the water keeps rising up to take it all back.

articles.title: An ambassador in Ljubljana, but not in London: Israel’s foreign policy shifts away from longstanding allies
articles.summary: As traditional partners in Western Europe lose patience with the settlement expansion and surging violence in the West Bank, Israel is cultivating ties elsewhere.
articles.body: Gideon Saar smiled as he cut the blue ribbon outside the newly inaugurated embassy of Nauru in Jerusalem. Israel’s foreign minister described the tiny Pacific island nation of some 12,000 people as “one of Israel’s greatest friends in the international community.” Two days later, it was Slovenia’s turn, as Saar cut the ribbon on a new embassy in Ljubljana. He praised the new center-right government for standing by Israel in the European Union, especially after the country had previously been one of Israel’s harshest critics. A large business delegation was brought along to show appreciation. There was no such celebration in London, where Israel faced one of its sharpest diplomatic rebukes in years: a coordinated move by the United Kingdom and 11 other countries to impose sanctions and trade restrictions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. Israel has had no ambassador in London for nearly a year. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s intended envoy, his chief of staff Tzachi Braverman, was barred from leaving Israel due to a criminal investigation, leaving the post vacant. The split-screen moment reflects a broader pattern in Israel’s foreign relations: As traditional partners in Western Europe grow distant, losing patience with the settlement expansion and surging violence in the West Bank, the right-wing government is cultivating ties with smaller or what it sees as more ideologically aligned countries, redirecting its diplomatic energy to other arenas. UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband tied the new measures, announced in parliament on Tuesday, directly to Israel’s decision to push ahead with the E1 settlement project, which critics say would cut the West Bank in two and close off the possibility of a contiguous future Palestinian state. But the move is part of a longer-term shift. In September 2025, Britain, Canada, France and more than a dozen other Western states recognized Palestinian statehood. And this June, the UK, Canada, France, Norway, Australia and New Zealand announced a wave of coordinated sanctions targeting individuals and networks accused of financing and enabling settler violence. Some of the states announced additional punitive measures: France barred far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich from entering the country, Italy opened an investigation into National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir over the treatment of detained activists, including Italians, after Israel intercepted an aid flotilla on its way to Gaza. The Netherlands declared both Ben Gvir and Smotrich “persona non grata” and approved its own ban on imports of settlement goods. Not every proposal has succeeded, and Israel has so far managed to stall broader actions from the EU. For years, Israel used Viktor Orban’s government in Hungary to block EU measures. Now, following a change in leadership in Budapest, Slovenia has effectively taken Hungary’s place as Israel’s representative in Brussels. A push by France and Sweden for an EU ban on settlement trade was stalled, as were efforts to expel Israel from the EU’s flagship Horizon research program. Dr. Rémi Daniel, from Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies (INSS) says the one comfort for Israel is that Germany and Italy have so far stuck to statements rather than joining the sanctions. “They are the most important EU member states because they have the power to block plans at the European level,” he said. But the trend was still concerning, he said, because looking at the balance of power within the EU, “the swinging center is going more against Israel.” Even as ties with some Western European allies fray, others are deepening their alliance with Israel through defense trade. Last month, Israel signed a $3.5 billion air-defense deal with Greece, one of the largest arm agreements in Israel’s history. And in early 2026, Israel Aerospace Industries signed a $3.1 billion deal with Germany to expand its supply of Arrow missile interceptor systems. Israel’s response to the new sanctions – and its attitude towards one of its oldest allies in general - has been openly combative. Saar swiftly announced he would close the British Consulate General in Jerusalem, end UK training for Palestinian Authority security forces, and ban entry to a dozen British officials and lawmakers. “The British move is morally distorted and constitutes a blatant interference in the affairs of a sovereign state and its electoral process,” Saar said Tuesday. Netanyahu labeled the UK the “Islamic Republic of Britain” on a podcast last month and has accused French President Emanuel Macron of fueling antisemitism by recognizing a Palestinian state. While relations with some Western allies cool, and even the friendly Trump administration in the United States appears to be growingly frustrated with settler violence, Israel has been pouring energies into other regions and redrawing its map of relationships. Declaring 2026 “The Year of South America,” Saar has toured Argentina, Ecuador, Paraguay and Colombia and restored relations with Bolivia, Chile and Honduras. He also opened a communication channel with Venezuela for the first time since 2009, sending rescue teams to assist with earthquake relief last month. New Israeli embassies opened in Zambia, Estonia, Moldova, Fiji and Slovenia. And Israel became the first country in the world to recognize the self-declared Republic of Somaliland as an independent state. Somaliland then opened an embassy in Jerusalem, where fewer than 10 countries have embassies, including the US. Argentina, Colombia, Costa Rica and the Democratic Republic of Congo have declared their intent to join the list. Daniel Shek, a former Israeli ambassador to France, argues that this pivot comes at a real cost and says the government is damaging relationships built over decades on shared interests in economy, science, culture, security. “They are sacrificing the alliances with the most significant countries,” he said. “If Saar thinks the Paraguayan economy can replace France as a partner for export and import, good for him.” The countries involved in the sanctions, he said, are not ideologically hostile to Israel, just its actions under Netanyahu, Ben Gvir and Smotrich. “France, Britain, Italy, the Netherlands, are friendly countries fed up with this Israeli government’s behavior.” Shek notes that the sanctions target the settlements, and not Israel itself, and that their practical bite, for now, is limited. Still, he says, they should not be underestimated. “Once sanctions have been imposed, it is significant,” he said. “There are things that have been opened and cannot be put back in the bottle.”

articles.title: Mahira Khan is becoming a mother again: Why the second pregnancy can feel completely different from the first
articles.summary: The second pregnancy can arrive with a strange sense of déjà vu: the growing belly, the appointments, the anticipation of meeting a baby again. Yet fo.
articles.body: The second pregnancy can arrive with a strange sense of déjà vu: the growing belly, the appointments, the anticipation of meeting a baby again. Yet for many mothers, it can also feel like entering an entirely different version of pregnancy. The body remembers, the mind has changed, and there is already a child waiting at home.That is the interesting part of Mahira Khan's pregnancy announcement. The Pakistani actor, who is 41, announced at the Toronto International Film Festival that she is expecting her second child with husband Salim Karim. She already has a son, Azlan, from her previous marriage.A second pregnancy isn't simply a repeat of the first. Research increasingly suggests that the experience can be different physically, psychologically and even neurologically.Your brain may respond differently the second timeOne of the newest findings comes from a 2026 study examining how a second pregnancy affects women's brains. Researchers found that a second pregnancy produced distinct changes in brain structure and neural networks, rather than simply repeating the pattern seen during a first pregnancy. The findings suggest that the brain adapts not only to pregnancy itself but also to the experience of becoming a mother again.That matters because a first pregnancy means preparing for an entirely unfamiliar role. By a second pregnancy, there is already a lived experience of pregnancy, childbirth and caring for a newborn. The mother isn't entering motherhood for the first time. She is expanding an existing family.The researchers described the second pregnancy as involving its own pattern of neural adaptation, adding to evidence that pregnancy-related brain changes are not identical from one pregnancy to another.The emotions can change tooThe emotional landscape of a second pregnancy can be complicated.There may be excitement about giving an older child a sibling, but also questions that did not exist the first time: Will I be able to love another child in the same way? How will my older child react? Can I manage two children? What happens to the relationship I already have with my firstborn?A 2026 study examining anxiety, stress and psychological resources among women experiencing a second pregnancy found that many participants experienced moderate anxiety, highlighting that being pregnant again does not automatically mean feeling more relaxed or emotionally prepared.In other words, experience can make some things easier while creating entirely new worries.The first pregnancy is about becoming a mother. The second is about becoming a mother of two.That difference may be one of the biggest psychological shifts.During a first pregnancy, much of the anticipation centres on the unknown: What will labour feel like? What will the baby be like? How will life change?During a second pregnancy, there is already a child whose routine, emotions and needs continue alongside the pregnancy.That means the pregnancy can feel less like waiting for a single life-changing event and more like gradually reorganising an entire family.What Mahira Khan's announcement reminds parents aboutMahira's announcement is ultimately a personal milestone, not evidence that her pregnancy will follow any particular pattern. But it opens the door to a broader parenting conversation.A second pregnancy isn't a replay of the first. There is a different body, a different stage of life, an older child, a different family dynamic and a brain that has already experienced pregnancy and motherhood.For some women, that can mean more confidence. For others, it can bring a different kind of anxiety. For many, it can be both at the same time.And perhaps that is why the second pregnancy can feel so unfamiliar despite being something a mother has technically experienced before: the baby may be new, but the woman carrying that baby is not the same person she was the first time.Looking for trusted parenting advice? articles.title: One dead, 102 rescued from Indonesian ferry that went missing in Java Sea
articles.summary: The nation's search and rescue team said it lost contact with the Virgo Transport 8 in the early hours of Sunday morning.
articles.body:
One person has died and 102 have been rescued from a stricken Indonesian ferry that went missing after encountering bad weather in the Java Sea, an official said.

A search and rescue operation was launched after contact was lost with the Virgo Transport 8 ship as it took 243 people from Surabaya to the south Kalimantan city of Banjarmasin in the early hours of Sunday, Indonesia's search and rescue agency said.

The search for the remaining passengers is ongoing.

The ferry was last reported to be in the Java Sea about 150km south of Banjarmasin around 02:00 local time on Sunday.

articles.title: 1,400 Yemenis flee to Djibouti within 24 hours
articles.summary: Yemeni refugees arrive in Obock, Djibouti, within 24 hours as Houthis tighten their grip on the Bab al-Mandeb strait.
articles.body:
About 1,400 people have fled Yemen for Djibouti in a 24-hour period, Djibouti’s economy and finance minister says, as Houthi fighters tighten their grip on the Bab al-Mandeb strait.

Ilyas Moussa Dawaleh wrote on X on Saturday: “1,400 refugees arrived in Djibouti from Yemen in just 24 hours.”

In a separate post on Friday, the minister said that 500 refugees had arrived in the coastal city of Obock, including women and children, after they were rescued at sea when their boats ran out of fuel while crossing the Bab-el-Mandeb strait.

Obock, a city only about 20 kilometres (12 miles) across the water from the Yemeni coast, has for several years been a preferred arrival point for those seeking refuge from war-torn Yemen. The Bab-el-Mandeb strait is also used in the opposite direction by migrants from the Horn of Africa, who transit through Yemen on their way to Gulf countries.

Safiya Ibrahim, humanitarian response coordinator for the International Organization for Migration (IOM), told AFP that “vulnerable groups such as women and children have reached the shores of Obock, with more expected in the coming days”.

The IOM warned on Friday that at least 46,000 people had been displaced in Yemen since fighting escalated last week.

“Families are being forced to flee for the second or third time in this conflict, with almost nothing left,” Amy Pope, the IOM director general, said in a statement. “As fighting spreads, reaching people with lifesaving assistance is becoming harder. We urgently need safe, unimpeded access.”

Djibouti hosts tens of thousands of refugees and asylum seekers. United Nations Refugee Agency figures from March 2026 show a registered population of more than 36,000, with the majority from Somalia, Ethiopia and Yemen.

The Houthis seized the Red Sea port city of Mocha on Thursday and have since overrun the coastline and islands surrounding the Bab al-Mandeb strait. The rapid offensive has forced thousands of families to flee, with entire villages reportedly emptied in districts such as Maqbanah, Jabal Habashi and al-Maafer.

articles.title: New York City warns of possible flash floods as thunderstorms develop along East Coast
articles.summary: Federal forecasters issued flood alerts for 39 million people late Saturday into Sunday as a line of thunderstorms developed from Washington, D.C., to New Haven, Connecticut.
articles.body: Federal forecasters issued flood alerts for 39 million people late Saturday into Sunday as a line of thunderstorms developed from Washington, D.C., to New Haven, Connecticut. New York City Emergency Management warned residents of heavy rain and possible flash flooding into Sunday morning as the city opened 51 weather shelters for those vulnerable to floodwaters, including people in basement apartments. The National Weather Service issued a slew of flood alerts, including flood watches, late Saturday through early Sunday for parts of Maryland, Pennsylvania, Delaware and New Jersey. A flood watch for Washington, D.C., expired at 1 a.m. Sunday. Philadelphia and neighboring counties were under a flood watch through morning. A flood watch for New York City was scheduled to start at 4 a.m. Sunday and extend through noon. New York City Emergency Management said in a statement that 5 to 7 inches of rain could fall in Nassau and Suffolk counties, as well as in southern Connecticut, and warned that the city’s eastern boroughs could also be hit with heavy rain. “A small shift in where the rain sets up would bring 5 to 7 inch totals and a much higher flash flooding risk into eastern Brooklyn and Queens,” it said. “New Yorkers in those neighborhoods living in basements and below grade are urged to move to higher ground tonight.” A flood watch for parts of southern Connecticut, including northern New Haven, was in effect through Sunday afternoon, according to the weather service. The thunderstorms are emerging as a trough of cold air high in the atmosphere moves east and clashes with warmer air, federal forecasters said. “The combination of instability, deep moisture, and forcing, may lead to an elevated threat for excessive rainfall and severe thunderstorms,” the weather service said in a forecast discussion late Saturday.
